_about: Content for the clickable body map. Each system lists which indicators drive its colour, what spaceflight does to it, which NASA HRP hazards cause it, and countermeasures. System colour = worst tier among its indicators.

systems.name: Heart & blood vessels
systems.function: Pumps blood carrying oxygen and nutrients around the body.
spaceflight_effects: Fluids shift toward the head; blood volume drops and crews are chronically mildly dehydrated.
24 h blood pressure falls ~8-10 mmHg in flight as blood vessels relax.
On return to gravity, blood pools in the legs - dizziness or fainting risk (orthostatic intolerance).
countermeasures: Thigh cuffs to limit head-ward fluid shift (under study)

systems.name: Bones & muscles
systems.function: Supports the body and lets you move. Bones also store calcium.

derived_metrics.est_bone_loss_pct: Modelled: hip/spine areal BMD loss of 1-1.5% per month without adequate exercise. App estimates cumulative loss from days in flight x (1 - exercise compliance factor). Tiers: green <=6%, amber 6-10%, red >10% (6% ~ a typical 6-month ISS mission).
derived_metrics.est_calf_muscle_loss_pct: Modelled: ~13% calf volume loss over 6 months on ISS despite exercise. Tiers: green <=10%, amber 10-15%, red >15%.

spaceflight_effects: Bone mineral density drops ~1-1.5% per month at weight-bearing sites (hip, spine, legs).
Hip trabecular bone lost 2.2-2.7%/month in a CT study of 14 ISS crew.
Calf muscle volume fell ~13% over 6 months even with exercise; slow-twitch fibres lost >40% power.
Calcium leaving bone passes through the kidneys, raising the risk of kidney stones.
countermeasures: Adequate protein, eaten soon after exercise
systems.measurement_note: Bone density cannot be measured daily in flight (needs DXA/CT scans), so the app shows a modelled estimate driven by exercise compliance and flags it for post-flight confirmation.

systems.name: Immune system
spaceflight_effects: Stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) rise and suppress immune cells.
Dormant herpes viruses reactivate: 61% of ISS astronauts studied shed one or more herpes viruses; reactivation rises with mission length.
Only a small share develop symptoms, but this is a growing risk for Mars-length missions.

systems.name: Eyes & brain pressure (SANS)
systems.function: Vision; the optic nerve links the eye to the brain.
spaceflight_effects: Blood and cerebrospinal fluid shift toward the head.
Signs include optic disc swelling, globe flattening, choroidal folds and a far-sighted (hyperopic) shift.
At least one SANS feature found in 81% of NASA astronauts after long-duration flight; worse with longer and repeat missions.

systems.name: Mind, mood & sleep
spaceflight_effects: ISS crews average ~6 h sleep despite 8.5 h scheduled; ~75% used sleep medication at some point.
Short sleep degrades vigilant attention and mood.
Isolation, confinement and long comms delays strain mood and crew relationships.
countermeasures: Consistent sleep schedule and light management

systems.name: Metabolism & nutrition
systems.function: Turns food into energy and building blocks.
spaceflight_effects: Signals of insulin resistance seen in astronauts (gene/pathway changes).
Body mass often decreases; appetite can be poor.
A 1 C rise in body temperature needs ~20% more energy from food.

systems.name: Body temperature
systems.function: Keeps the body's core temperature in a narrow, safe range.
spaceflight_effects: No convection in weightlessness, so heat is shed less efficiently.
Resting core temperature climbs to ~38 C over ~2.5 months; can exceed 40 C during exercise.
countermeasures: Use personal baseline, not 37 C, as 'normal'

systems.name: Lungs & breathing
systems.function: Brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide.
spaceflight_effects: Cabin CO2 is far higher than on Earth (~0.23 mmHg outdoors). NASA limits the 1-hour average to 3 mmHg; crews report symptoms from about 2.3 mmHg and headaches between 2.8 and 4.5 mmHg.
sources: NASA HRP hostile closed environment hazard (see challenge Resources tab)
